function.name: system_command
function.description: Run one command from a fixed allow-list. Do NOT use this to read, write, list, or search files, to get the current directory, or to find an executable — use file_read_full, file_read_lines, file_write_full, dir_list, file_find_glob, grep_files, dir_current, or find_executable instead; they are more reliable and this tool cannot do those things (cat, head, tail, ls, find, grep, pwd, and which are not available here). What this tool is for: running a build/lint/vet tool for the project's language: gofmt, golangci-lint, go build, go vet, go fmt (Go); cargo build, cargo check, cargo clippy, cargo fmt (Rust); tsc, eslint, prettier (JS/TS); javac (Java); gcc, clang, cppcheck, clang-tidy (C/C++); flake8, pylint, ruff, mypy (Python); or ps for process inspection. go and cargo only work with those exact subcommands — go run, cargo install, and similar are not allowed. This is not a full shell — the only supported operator is && to chain commands (each one only runs if the previous one succeeded, same as a shell). There is no piping, redirection, ;, ||, command substitution, or backgrounding: anything else after a command name is passed to it literally, so operators like | or > will not work and will just be treated as plain text arguments.

command.description: One command and its arguments, or several joined by &&, e.g. "go build ./... && go vet ./...". No other shell operators.

function.name: dir_current
function.description: dir_current returns the current working directory.

function.name: find_executable
function.description: find_executable looks up the full path of an executable program by name, searching the same locations a shell would use. Returns an error if no such executable is found.

name.description: The name of the executable to look up, e.g. "go" or "python3".
